title: Sorting Algorithms: Divide & Conquer
summary: Introduces divide and conquer: split a problem into smaller copies of itself, solve them, then combine the results. Merge Sort is the example: split the list into single items, then merge sorted pieces back together, for O(n log n) time. The lesson shows an iterative version and says the recursive version comes later. Step-by-step guide arrives when the lecture is published.
goal: Explain how Merge Sort divides and merges, and why it runs in O(n log n).

steps.title: Read the lesson
steps.detail: Read the Merge Sort page, especially the 'Divide and Conquer Algorithms' and 'Implementation Breakdown' sections.
steps.doneWhen: You can name the three steps: divide, conquer, combine.

steps.title: Run the merge step on its own
steps.detail: merge() is the heart of Merge Sort. Copy it from the lesson and run it on two sorted lists.
steps.code:
def merge(left, right):
    result = []
    i, j = 0, 0
    while i < len(left) and j < len(right):
        if left[i] < right[j]:
            result.append(left[i])
            i += 1
        else:
            result.append(right[j])
            j += 1
    result.extend(left[i:])
    result.extend(right[j:])
    return result

print(merge([1, 4, 5], [2, 3, 6]))

steps.title: Trace the iterative version
steps.detail: Run the lesson's merge_sort_iterative on [2, 8, 5, 3, 9, 4, 1, 7] and print the list each time sublist_len doubles (1, 2, 4).
steps.doneWhen: You see sorted pairs, then sorted fours, then the fully sorted list.

steps.title: Explain why it's n log n
steps.detail: Interview practice: say it out loud before coding. The list halves about log n times, and each level merges all n items, so time is O(n log n). The merged lists need O(n) extra space.
steps.doneWhen: You can explain the Big-O and space cost in two sentences.

concepts.meaning: Break a problem into smaller copies of itself, solve them, combine the answers.
Combine two sorted lists into one sorted list by repeatedly taking the smaller front item.
Sort by splitting into single items and merging them back in order.
About log n rounds of splitting, with n items of work in each round.
